summary: We built a simple web map that shows where Pune has lost vegetation since 2000. Using NASA MODIS vegetation data (NDVI, March to May, 2000 to 2024), we worked out how greenness changed at every 1 km pixel across Pune district. The district as a whole got greener, but a few cells in east Pune, around Kharadi and Manjri, lost roughly 36 to 39 percent of their pre-monsoon vegetation. The map is full screen. You can hover anywhere to read the trend and click a hotspot to zoom in. It speaks to the challenge by turning 25 years of Earth observation data into something anyone can read in a few seconds. It matters because green cover helps with heat, air quality and drainage, and it's easier to protect before it's gone than after. It runs in the browser with no login and no keys.
details:
What it does

The project is a static web page with a full-screen map and a small side panel. The map shows the NDVI trend (change in vegetation per decade) for Pune district at 1 km resolution. Hover anywhere to read the value at that spot. The panel also has a time series of district-mean NDVI, a list of urban hotspots you can click to zoom to, a dark and satellite basemap switch, and an opacity slider.

How it works

We used NASA MODIS Terra MOD13A3 NDVI from 2000 to 2024 in Google Earth Engine. For each year we took the March to May mean, which is the dry pre-monsoon window, so monsoon timing doesn't mess up the comparison. Then for every pixel we fit a straight line through the 25 yearly values. The slope is the change per decade and that's the map layer. We also averaged the data into 1 km cells, measured change against each cell's 2000 to 2004 baseline, and ranked them. Cells within 15 km of central Pune count as urban. Two of the top five cells were far out in rural areas, so we left them out of the headline.

What we found

District mean NDVI went from about 0.28 to about 0.36, so the district got greener overall. But three cells in east Pune near Kharadi and Manjri lost about 36 to 39 percent of their vegetation over the same period. That's the area known for fast IT park and housing growth, though we haven't proven that's the cause.

What we left out

We also tried land surface temperature to get at urban heat. The results showed cooling almost everywhere, which doesn't make sense for a growing city, and we couldn't figure out why in the time we had. We decided not to report a result we couldn't trust, so the app only shows vegetation and says temperature is under review.

Benefits and impact

The goal is to make long-term satellite trends easy to read. Planners, residents or students can see where green cover is dropping without opening a GIS tool. The approach isn't specific to Pune, but we only ran Pune here.

Tools

Google Earth Engine for the NASA data, Python (numpy, pandas, Pillow) to prepare the data, and plain HTML, JavaScript and Leaflet for the map. It's hosted as a static site on GitHub Pages. Basemaps are from Esri and OpenStreetMap contributors. Claude (Anthropic) was used for code and drafting, as described in the SI section.

What's creative about it

We kept it as small as we could: one page, no backend, no accounts, no API keys, and the hover readout shows the raw trend instead of hiding it behind a chart. We also chose to drop a result we couldn't validate instead of building a nicer story around it.

What we considered

1 km pixels aren't neighborhoods, so cell names are approximate. NDVI loss isn't the same as construction, since farmland changes on the city edge can look similar. Rainfall changes NDVI a lot between years and we didn't control for it. The trend test is basic and ignores year-to-year correlation. We wrote these limits into the methodology file in the repo.
